title: Love Her Again: The Wife Bought Back
summary: God tells Hosea to go and love his adulterous wife again, as the LORD loves Israel even though they turn to other gods. Hosea buys her back for silver and barley and tells her that she must live with him many days in faithfulness before their marriage resumes. So Israel will live many days without king, sacrifice, or idols, and afterward will return to seek the LORD and David their king in the last days.
story: This short chapter is the hinge of Hosea's opening section. Chapter 1 told of the marriage and children in the third person; chapter 2 spoke of God's case against Israel and his promise to woo her back; chapter 3 returns to Hosea's household, now told in his own voice, and acts out that promise. The wife has left, and the story has reached what seems its end. God's command reopens it. The chapter then compresses Israel's future into two verses: a long period of deprivation, which history filled with the Assyrian exile of the north and later the Babylonian exile of the south, and a return to God and to a king from David's line. The oracles of chapters 4 to 14 will explain why the discipline is necessary.
historical:
The chapter's first-person narrative gives no date, but it belongs to Hosea's ministry in the northern kingdom in the second half of the eighth century BC. The prediction that Israel would live many days without king or prince came true in stages. After Jeroboam II, the throne changed hands by assassination repeatedly, and in 722 BC the kingdom ended altogether with the Assyrian capture of Samaria and the deportation of much of its population (2 Kings 17:5-6). The northern tribes never again had a king of their own.

The mention of David their king is striking in a prophecy to the north. The northern tribes had rejected David's dynasty two centuries earlier with the cry, as 1 Kings 12:16 records, that they had no share in David. Hosea's hope is that the divided people will return not only to the LORD but also to the royal line God chose. Some scholars think this phrase was added when Hosea's book was preserved in Judah; others note that it fits 1:11, where Israel and Judah appoint one leader, and that Amos, Hosea's contemporary, also looked for the restoration of David's fallen house (Amos 9:11).
cultural:
The price Hosea pays, fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley, is a mix of money and goods. A shekel was a weight of silver (about 11 grams), not yet a coin. A homer was a large dry measure, commonly estimated at around 200 liters, though ancient measures are uncertain; the lethech is mentioned only here and was probably half a homer. Some interpreters calculate that the total roughly equaled thirty shekels, the compensation price of a slave in Exodus 21:32, but the value of barley in shekels at the time is not known precisely. Payment in part in barley may suggest that Hosea did not have the full price in silver. Why a payment was needed is not explained: she may have been in debt slavery, in the household of another man, or bound to service at a shrine.

Verse 4 lists the institutions Israel will lose. King and prince are the political order. Sacrifice and the sacred pillar (a standing stone set up at shrines, forbidden in Deuteronomy 16:22 but common in Israel's worship) are the religious order. The ephod was a priestly garment sometimes used in seeking guidance from God (1 Samuel 23:9-12), and teraphim, translated idol here, were household images, possibly of ancestors, also used in divination. The list mixes legitimate and illegitimate things: exile will strip away both. Raisin cakes (verse 1) were festive food, eaten at celebrations and apparently offered in the worship of other gods.
literary: The chapter is a short first-person prophetic report, like the sign actions of Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, in which a prophet performs an act and then explains it. The structure is a pair: command and obedience (verses 1-3), then interpretation (verses 4-5). The word love appears four times in verse 1, tying Hosea's love for his wife to the LORD's love for Israel and exposing the false loves of both. The repetition of many days in verses 3 and 4 links the wife's period of waiting with Israel's time without king and sacrifice, and the word afterward in verse 5 marks the turn from discipline to restoration.

outline.t: Hosea buys her back and sets a time of waiting
Israel's many days without king or sacrifice
Afterward they will return to the LORD and to David their king

doctrines.note: God's love for Israel persists though they turn to other gods (verse 1). It is not naive; it includes discipline and waiting. But it takes the initiative and pays a price to restore the relationship.
Hosea buys back a woman who had left him. The chapter is an image of redemption: a costly act by the wronged party to bring back the one who was lost.

Afterward the people will return and seek the LORD. Return is the fruit of God's prior love and discipline, and it is described as coming trembling to God and to his goodness, a mixture of awe and trust.
Israel will seek David their king in the last days. This is part of the Old Testament's hope for a future king from David's line, which the New Testament applies to Jesus.

words.note: Ahav, to love. Verse 1 uses the verb four times: Hosea is to love his wife, who is loved by another, as the LORD loves Israel, who love raisin cakes. The word covers love between spouses, parents and children, and God and his people. Here the difference between God's love and false loves is the whole point: his love is faithful when theirs is not.

Naaph, to commit adultery, the verb of the seventh commandment (Exodus 20:14). The wife is called an adulteress, meaning a married woman who has been unfaithful. Hosea uses the word for Israel's covenant unfaithfulness as well as for literal adultery in the land (4:2, 13-14).

Shuv, to turn or return, one of Hosea's key words. In verse 5 Israel will return and seek the LORD. The word describes both repentance and the homecoming from exile, and Hosea often holds the two together: turning back to God is the road home.

christ: Verse 5 is one of several Old Testament texts that promise a future David, meaning a king from his line, after the exile (compare Jeremiah 30:9; Ezekiel 34:23-24). The New Testament presents Jesus as that king, the son of David (Matthew 1:1; Luke 1:32-33). The chapter's central act also foreshadows the gospel. Hosea's purchase of an unfaithful wife echoes the biblical language of redemption, buying back someone who is lost or enslaved, and the New Testament uses that language for Christ's death, by which believers were bought at a price (1 Corinthians 6:20; 1 Peter 1:18-19). The parallel is one of pattern, not prediction: Hosea shows in a household what God would do for the world in his Son, who loved his people while they were still unfaithful (Romans 5:8).

hard.q: Is the woman in chapter 3 Gomer, and why must she wait?
hard.a:
The text says only your wife, or literally a woman, loved by another. Most interpreters, ancient and modern, take her to be Gomer, now gone after other men, and read the chapter as the sequel to chapter 1: the husband pursues and restores the wife who left him, exactly as God promises in chapter 2. Some scholars think she is a different woman and that chapter 3 is a second sign act, or an alternative account of the same marriage told in the first person. The word again in verse 1 most naturally points to a renewed love for someone already loved, which favors the first view.

The period of waiting in verse 3 is a time of restraint in which she will not be with another man, and Hosea will be the same toward her. It is not rejection but preparation, a time for the old attachments to be broken before the marriage is fully restored. The application to Israel explains it: the nation must live many days without king, sacrifice, and idols before it can return to God with a whole heart.

questions: God tells Hosea to love a wife who has betrayed him. What does this chapter reveal about the cost of God's love?
Israel had to live many days without the things it relied on before it could return. Has God ever taken something away in order to draw you back to himself?
The people come trembling to the LORD and to his goodness. How can awe and trust belong together in the same response to God?
